atoms.text: The first enslaved Africans were brought to North America in 1619 via the Transatlantic Slave Trade. Over 12 million Africans were enslaved and transported across the Atlantic for over 250 years. In the southern colonies, they were forced to work on cotton and sugar plantations, while in the north many worked as domestic servants, artisans, or dock labourers.

American economy was heavily dependent on this labour so enslaved people were central to the growth of colonial wealth. “Slaves” were legally defined as property, could be sold and bought as such. While the slave trade was abolished in 1808, slavery remained legal in the US until 1865.

atoms.text: After independence in 1776, the new United States regulated immigration mainly through citizenship laws. The Naturalization Act of 1790 limited citizenship to “free white persons” which excluded enslaved and free Black people.

The Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798 then gave the federal government power to detain and deport non-citizens from “hostile” nations. These laws created a difference between legal citizens and immigrants and clearly favoured white European settlers.
